lessons.title: The human person and the family
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — The individual, the family and the community (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the characteristics of the human person
Define the family and distinguish nuclear and extended families
Explain the roles of the family and the rights and duties of its members
Explain the importance of moral values
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify definitions of family types used in the syllabus and the list of rights/duties of children; the content is intentionally general and non-prescriptive about family structures.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: A **human person** has body, mind and feelings; can think, choose and speak; has dignity and rights; and lives with others. Every person is **unique**, has needs (food, shelter, health, education, love, safety) and responsibilities towards others. A person grows through the family, school, friends, community and religion.

items.text: A family: grandparents, parents and children

blocks.caption: A family tree with grandparents, parents and children
blocks.alt: Boxes showing grandparents above parents above two children.

blocks.title: The family
blocks.md: The **family** is a group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption, who usually live together and support each other. A **nuclear family** is parents and their children. An **extended family** also includes grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins. In Cameroon the extended family is very important and gives support in many ways.

blocks.title: Roles of the family
blocks.md: The family gives **love and security**; provides **food, shelter, clothing and health care**; teaches **language, values and customs** (socialisation); supports children's **education**; offers **religious and moral guidance**; and helps members in difficulty (illness, bereavement, unemployment).

**Rights and duties in the family.** Children have the right to be cared for, to go to school, to be protected from abuse and harmful work, and to be heard. Their duties are to respect and obey their parents and elders, help with household tasks and study hard. Parents have the duty to protect and educate children and to treat them fairly; they also have rights, such as respect from their children.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Rights come with duties: do not list only rights.
- A family is not only 'father, mother and children'; families may be single-parent, extended or adoptive.
- Moral values (honesty, respect, responsibility, solidarity, hard work) are not only for the home: they apply in school, at work and in public life.

blocks.title: Example 1: type of family
blocks.statement: Mr and Mrs Ngu live with their three children, and Mrs Ngu's mother, in Bamenda. What type of family is this?
steps: Parents and children make a nuclear family.
Adding a grandparent living in the same household extends it.
So this is an extended family.

blocks.title: Example 2: right and duty
blocks.statement: A girl has the right to go to school. State two duties she has in return.
steps: She should attend regularly and work hard.
She should respect teachers and other pupils and obey school rules.
blocks.answer: Attend regularly and work hard; respect teachers, pupils and rules.

lessons.title: The citizen: rights and duties
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Citizenship Education — The individual, the family and the community (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the main rights and duties of a citizen
Explain why rights and duties go together
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: the ways nationality can be acquired under the Cameroonian nationality law (the lesson is deliberately general), and the list of rights and duties to match the syllabus wording.

Draft for teacher review: only widely accepted facts are used and the tone is neutral; the national symbols, institutions, legal ages and any health or legal statement must be verified before release. No political opinions are expressed.

blocks.md: A **citizen** is a member of a state who has legal rights and duties. **Citizenship** can be acquired by birth to a citizen parent, by birth in the country in some cases, by marriage or by a legal process called naturalisation, according to the nationality law. The citizen belongs to the national community and is protected by the state.

blocks.caption: Rights and duties go together
blocks.alt: Two boxes of rights and duties joined by a double arrow.

blocks.title: Rights of a citizen
blocks.md: Rights are what a person is entitled to by law. Examples: the right to **life** and **personal security**, **education**, **health care**, **equality before the law**, **freedom of expression**, **freedom of religion**, **freedom of movement**, **protection of property**, and the right to **take part in public life**, including voting.

blocks.title: Duties of a citizen
blocks.md: Duties are what a citizen must do. Examples: **obey the laws**, **pay taxes**, **respect others' rights**, **protect public property and the environment**, **take part in elections and community life** when entitled, **defend the country** and work for national unity, and **report crime** to the authorities.

**Why they go together:** the state protects rights using money and services from taxes, and citizens must respect others' rights in turn. If everybody claimed rights without duties, life together would be impossible. **Active citizenship** means taking part: voting, joining associations, volunteering, helping neighbours, caring for the environment and speaking up peacefully on community issues.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Rights are not unlimited: they are limited by the rights of others and by the law.
- Duties are not only punishments: they build the common good.
- A good citizen does not wait for the government to do everything; communities also improve their own surroundings.

blocks.title: Example 1: right or duty?
blocks.statement: Classify: A) paying taxes; B) freedom of expression; C) the right to education; D) obeying traffic rules.
steps: Taxes and traffic rules are obligations: duties.
Freedom of expression and education are entitlements: rights.
So A and D are duties; B and C are rights.
blocks.answer: A duty, B right, C right, D duty.

blocks.title: Example 2: balance
blocks.statement: A student plays loud music at midnight in a neighbourhood. Which right of the neighbours is affected, and which duty is not respected?
steps: Neighbours have the right to rest and a peaceful environment.
The student has the duty to respect others' rights.
Freedom to play music does not include disturbing others.
blocks.answer: The neighbours' right to rest; the duty to respect others.
